overview: This broad map label covers many herding communities, not a single people or kingdom. Its imported 2000 to 100 BCE window includes only part of a much longer history. The outline also contains scattered fragments far into the Sahel and Horn of Africa; it cannot establish one shared culture or political territory. The examples here concentrate on documented central Saharan sites.

periods.title: Late Pastoral communities
periods.summary: In the Acacus region, seasonal herding continued amid increasingly dry conditions.

periods.title: Final Pastoral changes
periods.summary: Regional archaeology records cultivation experiments and changing burial traditions alongside herding.

periods.title: Different paths through the desert
periods.summary: Some oasis communities became part of the Garamantian world; mobile herding did not have one collective ending.

items.text: Wadi Tanezzuft in southwestern Libya retained an oasis long after surrounding landscapes dried. Water stored in the regional drainage system helped sustain settlement during the second and first millennia BCE. A desert was not uniformly waterless: knowing which valley still held moisture could matter as much as owning a herd.

Some Tanezzuft dwellings stood close to water even where flooding remained possible. Archaeologists found their traces buried in alluvial deposits, while burial monuments occupied the oasis fringe outside fertile ground. Living, growing food and remembering the dead used different parts of the same landscape.

Final Pastoral sites in Wadi Tanezzuft yielded hearths, storage pits, grinding equipment, stone hoes and gouges. Researchers interpret this combination as evidence that some herders also cultivated plants. The label “nomad” should not make us imagine that every family moved constantly or lived entirely on meat and milk.

Seasonal floods could leave moist ground for crops as the water retreated. A study of Tanezzuft and the Acacus proposes that this kind of cultivation helped connect pastoral life with later oasis farming. The surviving evidence suggests experiments and local adjustments, rather than one sudden invention that transformed the whole Sahara.

Milk drinking has a much earlier Saharan history than this map window. At Takarkori, chemical traces absorbed into pottery show dairy processing during the fifth millennium BCE. Pots preserve more than shapes and decoration: tiny residues can keep evidence of a meal thousands of years after the washing-up.

At Afunfun TAG 9 in Niger, researchers recorded areas edged with stones and interpreted them as supports for tent or hut walls. Such modest remains are useful clues to shelter: a portable home may leave no standing walls, while the stones that steadied it stay behind.

At Iwelen in the Aïr Mountains, copper objects show metal use and perhaps working, but the investigators had not found smelting furnaces or slag. Other northern Niger sites did contain production evidence. Making a metal object, trading for one and extracting copper from ore are different achievements, with different archaeological traces.

The cemetery called site 96/129 in Wadi Tanezzuft preserves evidence of physically demanding lives near the end of the Late Pastoral sequence. Researchers examining the skeletons reported work-related bodily stresses. Bones cannot supply a person’s daily timetable, but they can reveal that ordinary labor left lasting marks.

At that same cemetery, some monuments contained multiple burials, burnt animal bones and small patches of ash. Investigators compared these with earlier burial traditions and the emerging Garamantian world. The findings show changing ways of treating the dead; they do not name the mourners or tell us exactly what people said.

In the Acacus, the Horse or Bitriangular art style includes domestic activities and social gatherings as well as herding, hunting and fighting. Researchers place these images broadly in the later pastoral and early Garamantian eras. Ancient artists chose many subjects; their world was more than a parade of cattle.

A painted chariot survives at the T-Afozzigiar-t rockshelter. It belongs to the Horse or Bitriangular artistic tradition, recognizable partly by stylized human bodies and horses. The picture is direct evidence of what an artist represented; its broad stylistic dating cannot identify an exact journey or battle.

Writing has to be treated separately from these pictures. Libyco-Berber inscriptions occur in the Acacus and are associated broadly with Garamantian and later history. They document regional writing, but the sources used here do not establish a securely translated inscription from the specific late prehistoric herding sites described above.

ending.text: There was no single fall of “Saharan pastoral nomads” in 100 BCE. Communities followed different paths as water, farming and political connections changed. In Tanezzuft, oasis settlement and Garamantian activity continued beyond this imported endpoint.
